author: Al Jazeera English
description:
Two activists from the Global Sumud Flotilla – Brazilian environmentalist Thiago Avila and Spanish national Saif Abu Keshek – have been detained by Israel after their boats were intercepted in international waters. The flotilla, carrying more than 170 activists and humanitarian aid, had set sail from Europe in April with the aim of breaking Israel's blockade on Gaza. Israeli naval forces seized 22 boats on 29 April, transferring the activists to Greek vessels; most were deported via Crete, but Avila and Abu Keshek were taken to Israel. Their lawyers say both men have been subjected to torture and violence, and their detention has sparked protests in several countries. Spain's prime minister has condemned Israel's actions as a violation of international law.

Al Jazeera’s Michael Appel reports.

Fighting is intensifying, despite a ceasefire that came into effect last month.
Israeli forces say they have carried out strikes on 120 Hezbollah targets, but the impact is being felt far beyond those sites. 
The health ministry says 41 people were killed in a 24-hour period over the weekend.
That's taken the total death toll since the beginning of March to more than 2,600.

Al Jazeera’s Rory Challands has more from Beirut, Lebanon.

Together with other Israeli-held areas, nearly two-thirds of Gaza is now under Israeli control.

description:
President Trump has warned the US will be withdrawing more troops from Germany.
The Pentagon ordered the initial drawdown of 5,000 on Friday from its largest European base.
Germany's defence minister says the move will encourage European nations to increase their own security. 
Trump threatened the withdrawal after Chancellor Friedrich Merz said the US was being “humiliated” by Iran. 
People in the German town of Landstuhl are worried about how the exit of US troops will affect them.
Some fear it will damage the local economy.

Al Jazeera’s Aksel Zaimovic reports.

Trita Parsi, executive vice president of the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft, says the US naval blockade of Iran has backfired on President Trump and is making the situation much worse.

“The negotiations were taking place and could have continued regardless of the blockade,” Parsi told Al Jazeera.

“The blockade has nothing to do with the Iranians being at the table. If anything, it is blocking diplomatic progress more than anything else.”

He argued that Trump had actually secured his greatest advantage through diplomacy before the blockade was imposed.

“Once he managed to get the ceasefire, the primary pressure on him, the war itself and the way it was pushing up gas prices, was lifted. Had he stayed in that scenario and used time to his advantage, he would have been in a much stronger position vis-a-vis the Iranians, because the Iranians had not managed to get the key thing they wanted: sanctions relief.”

author: Al Jazeera English
description:
Tensions surrounding potential US–Iran talks are increasingly driven by public messaging rather than real diplomatic progress.

Alex Vitena, senior fellow at the Middle East Institute, argues that both Washington and Tehran are engaging in “public posturing” instead of serious negotiations. He says there is still no agreement on even the basic framework of what talks should cover, making meaningful progress difficult.

According to him, the realistic path forward must focus on core issues—especially Iran’s nuclear program—while building trust through gradual, step-by-step diplomacy. He warns that expecting a quick or comprehensive deal after decades of conflict is unrealistic, and that media-driven narratives about “winning or losing” are undermining the process.

The video also highlights wider global consequences, including energy dependence on key routes like the Strait of Hormuz. Countries such as South Korea are already adapting by accelerating their shift toward renewable energy
title: Iran blockade crisis: Why It’s hurting the US

In central Tehran, a striking billboard targeting US President Donald Trump reflects growing political tension,  but for many Iranians, the real impact of the conflict is economic.

Despite a temporary ceasefire, daily life remains difficult as inflation surges and the national currency fluctuates. Prices of basic goods, from food items like eggs to cars, gold, and foreign currency, continue to rise, deepening anxiety among المواطنين.

Small business owners say years of sanctions, combined with recent conflict, have pushed the economy to a breaking point. Many fear that even if fighting does not resume, recovery could take years or even decades.

While some hope diplomacy could bring relief, others remain skeptical that negotiations will improve conditions in the short term. The ceasefire has paused direct violence, but for many, it has not delivered economic stability.
